You are an expert autonomous software engineer. Resolve the user issue with the smallest source change that satisfies the stated behavior.

The hidden grader applies your git diff to a fresh repository and runs its own tests. It never sees your reasoning. An empty diff scores zero. A correct source diff scores the task even if your local test was red or you never ran a test.

## Budget
You have 28 tool calls and 8 minutes. When either limit hits, the working tree is graded as it is. An edit made in time counts even if you do not reach submit_patch. Finish as soon as the edit is in so later tasks still have time.

## 1. Contract, before any tool call
Read the issue and keep a short list of the exact symbols, signatures, error strings, HTTP status codes, and return values it requires. Copy them character for character. The grader checks those strings exactly.

## 2. Locate in a few reads
- Search once with `git grep -n "SPECIFIC_TOKEN" -- '*.py' | head -20`. Use the most specific identifier or error string from the issue.
- Open only the matching region with `read_file`, at most 120 lines (`start_line` and `end_line`).
- You may do one follow-up grep or read if the first hit only re-exports the symbol.
- Do not page through unrelated files. Do not read a whole file when a range will do.

## 3. Edit by tool call 12
- By your 12th tool call a source file must already be edited. If it is not, edit the most likely function immediately. Runs that are still only reading after 12 calls almost never succeed.
- Prefer `edit_file`. `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation. Change the smallest span that implements the contract.
- If `edit_file` reports that `old_string` is not present ("mandatory input parameters are not present"), or fails twice on the same change because `old_string` was not found, do not resend it. Use the code-edit skill's `replace` mode: write the exact current lines to /tmp/old.txt and the new lines to /tmp/new.txt, each with one `run_command` heredoc (`cat > /tmp/new.txt <<'EOF'` ... `EOF`), then call `run_skill_script(skill_name="code-edit", file_path="scripts/edit.py", args=["replace", "path/file.py", "@/tmp/old.txt", "@/tmp/new.txt"])`. It matches despite escaping and refuses edits that would not parse.
- FastAPI documentation tasks: edit the executable example under `docs_src/`.
- Do not reformat or refactor unrelated code.
- Create a new file only when the issue explicitly requires a new module. Never create or edit `test_*.py`, `*_test.py`, anything under `tests/`, `pytest.ini`, or `conftest.py`.
- Any scratch script goes in `/tmp` through `run_command`. Never write scratch files into `/workspace`. Files left in the repository become part of the diff and fail grading.

## 4. One check, one repair, then submit
- After the edit, run at most one focused check: `pytest tests/test_file.py -k test_name -q` or `python -c "..."`.
- Never run bare `pytest`, `pytest .`, or `python -m unittest discover`.
- If that check fails with an assertion about the behavior you changed, apply one `edit_file` using the assertion text, then stop testing.
- If it fails because of missing fixtures, import errors, or pre-existing breakage, ignore it. Do not repair tests and do not install packages.
- Call `submit_patch` after that, even when the local check is red or you skipped it. A local green test is not the grader.
- If the diff contains a test path, run `git checkout --` on that path and call `submit_patch` again.
- If `get_status` shows less than 90 seconds remaining, call `submit_patch` immediately.

## Never
- Conclude that the code is already correct. Every task needs a source modification and a non-empty patch.
- Search outside `/workspace` (`/usr`, `/wheels`, `/opt`). Dependencies are already installed.
- Spend calls on broad exploration after the first edit.

You are evaluating a software engineering task for repository Textualize/rich.

Problem Statement:
Strip problematic private escape sequences

## Type of changes

- [x] Bug fix
- [ ] New feature
- [ ] Documentation / docstrings
- [ ] Tests
- [ ] Other

## Checklist

- [x] I've run the latest [black](https://github.com/psf/black) with default args on new code.
- [x] I've updated CHANGELOG.md and CONTRIBUTORS.md where appropriate.
- [x] I've added tests for new code.
- [x] I accept that @willmcgugan may be pedantic in the code review.

## Description

["Private escape sequences"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ANSI_escape_code#Fp_Escape_sequences) are escape sequences that are reserved for private use, though `\x1b7` and `\x1b8` are commonly used for storing and restoring the current cursor position. When those escape codes are not stripped the cursor jumps around and causes Rich to write garbage output. An example of a program that uses this cursor store/restore functionality is the APK package manager in Alpine Linux:

https://gitlab.alpinelinux.org/alpine/apk-tools/-/blob/48d91f482eb48a0a107b714ee183bb7e07782e14/src/print.c#L232-240

This commit updates the ANSI parser to ignore the `\x1b0`-`\x1b?` escape sequences, thus preventing them from being printed and causing havoc.

The regex `re_ansi` is:

```python
re_ansi = re.compile(
    r"""
(?:\\x1b\\](.*?)\\x1b\\\\)|\n(?:\\x1b([(@-Z\\\\-_]|\\[[0-?]*[ -/]*[@-~]))\n
    """,
    re.VERBOSE,
)
```

Wait, the `\n` in the `re.compile` call are actually part of the string because it's a triple-quoted string.

Let's look at the second part: `(?:\\x1b([(@-Z\\\\-_]|\\[[0-?]*[ -/]*[@-~]))`.
This matches `\x1b` followed by either:
1. A character in the range `(@-Z\_-)` (which is `(`, `@` to `Z`, `\`, `_` to `-`? No, `[` is not there).
2. `[` followed by some characters and then a character in the range `[@-~]`.

The problem statement says: "This commit updates the ANSI parser to ignore the `\x1b0`-`\x1b?` escape sequences".

`\x1b0` to `\x1b?` are characters with codes 48 to 63.
In ASCII:
'0' is 48
'?' is 63

The range `(@-Z\_-)` in the regex:
`(` is 40
`@` is 64
`Z` is 90
`\` is 92
`_` is 95
`-` is 45

Wait, `(@-Z\_-)` is a bit confusing. Let's see what it actually matches.
`@-Z` is 64-90.
`\_-` is 92 and 95-45? No, `\_-` probably means `\` and `_` and `-`.
Actually, `(@-Z\\-_]` means:
- `(`
- `@` through `Z`
- `\`
- `-`
- `_`

Wait, `\x1b0` to `\x1b?` are characters 48 to 63.
'0' is 48.
'?' is 63.
'(' is 40.
' ' is 32.

If the regex is `(?:\\x1b([(@-Z\\\\-_]|\\[[0-?]*[ -/]*[@-~]))`, then `\x1b0` would match if '0' is in `(@-Z\\-_]`.
'0' is 48. '@' is 64. So '0' is NOT in `@-Z`.
'(' is 40.
So `\x1b0` is NOT matched by `(@-Z\\-_]`.

Wait, if it's NOT matched by the regex, it will be treated as plain text.
The problem says "When those escape codes are not stripped the cursor jumps around and causes Rich to write garbage output."
This means they ARE being passed through as plain text and then printed to the terminal, where the terminal interprets them as escape sequences.

To "strip" them, we need to make the regex match them, and then ensure they are not yielded as plain text.

In `_ansi_tokenize`:

```python
    for match in re_ansi.finditer(ansi_text):
        start, end = match.span(0)
        osc, sgr = match.groups()
        if start > position:
            yield _AnsiToken(ansi_text[position:start])
        if sgr:
            if sgr == "(":
                position = end + 1
                continue
            if sgr.endswith("m"):
                yield _AnsiToken("", sgr[1:-1], osc)
        else:
            yield _AnsiToken("", sgr, osc)
        position = end
```

If `sgr` is matched, it's either:
- `(`: skipped.
- ends with `m`: yielded as SGR.
- otherwise: yielded as `_AnsiToken("", sgr, osc)`.

Wait, if `sgr` is yielded as `_AnsiToken("", sgr, osc)`, what happens to it?
Let's look at `AnsiDecoder.decode_line`.

In `decode_line`:

```python
        for plain_text, sgr, osc in _ansi_tokenize(line):
            if plain_text:
                append(plain_text, self.style or None)
            elif osc is not None:
                # ... handle osc ...
            elif sgr is not None:
                # ... handle sgr ...
```

If `sgr` is not None, it tries to parse it as a list of integers.
If `sgr` is something like `7` (for `\x1b7`), then `sgr.split(";")` is `['7']`.
`codes` will be `[7]`.
`SGR_STYLE_MAP[7]` is `"reverse"`.
So `\x1b7` would be interpreted as "reverse" style! That's definitely wrong. `\x1b7` is "Save cursor position".

Wait, the problem says `\x1b0` to `\x1b?` should be ignored.
'0' is 48, '?' is 63.
The current regex `re_ansi` is:
`r"(?:\\x1b\\](.*?)\\x1b\\\\)|\n(?:\\x1b([(@-Z\\\\-_]|\\[[0-?]*[ -/]*[@-~]))"`

Let's check the range `(@-Z\\-_]`.
`(` is 40.
`@` is 64.
`Z` is 90.
`\` is 92.
`-` is 45.
`_` is 95.

Wait, `(@-Z\\-_]` is a character class.
`@-Z` matches characters from 64 to 90.
`(` matches 40.
`\\` matches 92.
`-` matches 45.
`_` matches 95.

So it matches: 40, 45, 64-90, 92, 95.
It does NOT match 48-63 (`0-?`).

So `\x1b0` to `\x1b?` are currently NOT matched by the regex, and thus they are treated as `plain_text`.
When they are treated as `plain_text`, they are appended to the `Text` object and then printed to the terminal.
The terminal then sees `\x1b7` and saves the cursor position.

To fix this, we need to include `0-?` in the regex so that they are matched as `sgr` (or something else) and then ignored by `AnsiDecoder`.

If we add `0-?` to the character class: `([0-?@-Z\\-_])`? No, `0-?` is 48-63.
`(` is 40.
`0-?` is 48-63.
`@-Z` is 64-90.
So we can use `(0-?@-Z\\-_]`. Wait, `(` is still there.
`([0-?@-Z\\-_])` would match 48-90, 92, 95.
But we also want `(`.

So `([(0-?@-Z\\-_])`.
Wait, `(` is 40. `0` is 48.
So `([(0-?@-Z\\-_])` matches:
- `(` (40)
- `0` to `?` (48-63)
- `@` to `Z` (64-90)
- `\` (92)
- `_` (95)
- `-` (45)

Wait, the original was `([(@-Z\\\\-_]`.
`(` is 40.
`@-Z` is 64-90.
`\\` is 92.
`-` is 45.
`_` is 95.

If I change it to `([0-?@-Z\\-_])`, I lose `(` and `-`.
If I change it to `([(0-?@-Z\\-_])`, I have `(`, `0-?`, `@-Z`, `\`, `_`, `-`.
Wait, `-` in a character class needs to be at the beginning or end or escaped.
In `([(@-Z\\\\-_]`, the `-` is at the end: `\\-_]`. No, it's `\\-_]`.
Wait, `\\\\` is a literal backslash in the regex string.
So it's `[ ( @-Z \ - _ ]`.
Wait, `\\-` is an escaped hyphen.

Let's look at the regex again:
`r"(?:\\x1b\\](.*?)\\x1b\\\\)|\n(?:\\x1b([(@-Z\\\\-_]|\\[[0-?]*[ -/]*[@-~]))"`

The character class is `([(@-Z\\\\-_]`.
`(`
`@-Z`
`\\`
`-`
`_`

If I want to add `0-?`, I can do `([0-?@-Z\\\\-_])` but I need `(`.
So `([(0-?@-Z\\\\-_])`.
Wait, `0-?` is 48-63.
`(` is 40.
`-` is 45.
So `(0-?` is not a continuous range.

Let's try `([(0-?@-Z\\\\-_])`.
Wait, `0-?` is 48-63.
`(` is 40.
`-` is 45.
`@-Z` is 64-90.
`\` is 92.
`_` is 95.

So the characters are: 40, 45, 48-63, 64-90, 92, 95.
This can be written as `([(0-?@-Z\\\\-_])`.
Wait, `0-?` is 48-63. `@` is 64.
So `0-?@-Z` is actually `0-Z`!
`0` is 48. `Z` is 90.
So `[0-Z]` covers 48-90.
And we have `(`, `-`, `\`, `_`.

So `([(0-Z\\\\-_])` would cover:
- `(` (40)
- `0-Z` (48-90)
- `\` (92)
- `-` (45)
- `_` (95)

Wait, let's check if there are any characters between `(` (40) and `0` (48) that we WANT to match.
41: `)`
42: `*`
43: `+`
44: `,`
45: `-` (matched)
46: `.`
47: `/`

The original regex had `(` and `-`.
So it matched 40 and 45.
And 64-90, 92, 95.

If I use `([(0-Z\\\\-_])`, I match 40, 45, 48-90, 92, 95.
This includes 48-63 (`0-?`).

Wait, let's double check the range `0-?`.
'0' is 48.
'?' is 63.
